title: KNICKS DEADLINE CRISIS! Deuce & KAT Extension HOUR ZERO + $272M Question EXPLODES!
thumb_prompt: A giant countdown clock at Madison Square Garden showing 24:00 hours remaining, with two contract documents side by side on fire, dramatic orange and blue lighting casting shadows, urgent and tense atmosphere
thumb_subject: a determined point guard in a Knicks blue number two jersey standing next to a tall center in number thirty-two, both shown as silhouettes against the countdown clock

paragraphs.text: We are twenty four hours away from one of the most consequential deadlines in recent Knicks history. Tomorrow, August eleventh, is the cutoff date that will determine whether Deuce McBride and Karl-Anthony Towns can be traded during the twenty twenty seven season. And here's the thing that nobody is talking about loudly enough: neither one of them is signing an extension before that clock hits midnight. The Knicks are playing a high stakes game of chicken with their own championship roster, and the entire league is watching. This isn't just about money. This is about control, flexibility, and whether Leon Rose's front office is willing to lock itself into decisions it can't reverse. The silence from both camps is deafening. No leaks. No progress reports. Just the ticking clock.
card_lines: Neither expected to sign before deadline

paragraphs.text: Let me explain why this matters so much. Any veteran who signs an extension cannot be traded for six months. With the twenty twenty seven trade deadline set for February eleventh, tomorrow represents the last day either player could sign and still be movable by the deadline. Now, I'm not saying the Knicks want to trade either guy. But in the modern NBA, optionality is everything. We saw this play out with Mikal Bridges last summer. The Knicks extended him just under the six month cutoff, which kept them in the Giannis Antetokounmpo sweepstakes conversation. They didn't move Bridges, thank God, but they preserved the option. That's how championship front offices operate in this second apron hellscape.

Here's where it gets uncomfortable for Knicks fans. According to multiple reports, including Daily Knicks, if the team does not extend Deuce McBride by August eleventh, speculation about his future will go into hyperdrive. McBride is entering the final year of his criminally cheap three point nine million dollar contract. He's eligible for an extension worth up to ninety five million over four years. That's the max he can get. But here's the brutal reality: the Knicks' guard depth and James Dolan's second apron paranoia mean McBride's name keeps surfacing in trade rumors. He's the perfect salary filler for a bigger move. Young, productive, on an expiring deal, and just expensive enough to make the math work.
card_lines: Perfect trade chip for bigger deal

paragraphs.text: Now let's talk about the elephant in Madison Square Garden. Karl-Anthony Towns isn't signing anything tomorrow either. And it has nothing to do with whether he wants to stay in New York. Towns is eligible for a four year, two hundred seventy two point eight million dollar max extension. That number makes Jalen Brunson's discount look like a Nobel Prize in self sacrifice. According to James Edwards at The Athletic, the Knicks are not expected to offer Towns the full max. They're hoping he pulls a Brunson and takes less to keep the band together. But here's the problem: Towns has zero incentive to sign before August eleventh. Even if he trusts the organization, waiting until after tomorrow strips away any possibility of being traded mid season. It's the smart play for him, and his agent knows it.
card_lines: Knicks unlikely to offer full amount

paragraphs.text: Every conversation about Towns' extension comes back to Jalen Brunson. In twenty twenty four, Brunson left one hundred thirteen million dollars on the table by signing a one hundred fifty six point five million dollar extension instead of waiting for his full max. That decision, which seemed insane at the time, directly enabled the Knicks to build the roster that won the twenty twenty six championship. Brunson bet on himself, bet on the organization, and won a ring two years later. Now the Knicks are asking Towns to do the same thing. And I get why that feels reasonable to the front office. But here's the uncomfortable truth: Brunson was a homegrown star who chose New York. Towns was traded here and delivered immediately. Those are different psychological situations.

The expectation around the league is that Towns will have to take significantly less than his max to stay. Some reports suggest the Knicks might offer something around fifty million per year, totaling two hundred million over four years. That would save the team over seventy million dollars and lower his twenty twenty seven to twenty eight cap number by more than ten million. It sounds like a discount, but it's still a massive payday. The question is whether Towns sees it that way, or whether he looks at Brunson's sacrifice and thinks, I already proved myself. I already won you a championship. Why should I be the second guy to take a haircut? That's the tension simmering beneath the surface as we count down to midnight tomorrow.

Let's not forget what Towns just accomplished. He averaged twenty point one points and eleven rebounds during the regular season, then helped the Knicks finish a five game Finals demolition of San Antonio. He defended Victor Wembanyama in one of the toughest individual matchups imaginable and thrived. He ripped down the biggest rebounds of his career. This wasn't a role player catching a ride to a ring. This was a two way star doing exactly what the Knicks traded for. And now they're asking him to take less than market value because the owner went on sports radio and declared the second apron a suicide mission. I'm not saying Towns should demand every dollar. But I understand why his camp isn't rushing to the table.

Deuce McBride is one of the most underrated players in the NBA. Bleacher Report just ranked him fifth among the league's most underrated guys, behind only Ty Jerome, Ryan Rollins, Nickeil Alexander-Walker, and Neemias Queta. Over the past two seasons, the Knicks have been five point four points better per one hundred possessions with him on the floor. He ranks in the ninety third percentile of defensive matchup difficulty and the ninety ninth percentile of three point shot making, according to BBall Index. The only other player in the league doing both? Max Christie. Deuce is a unicorn role player. And the Knicks might lose him because of a spreadsheet.

Here's the cold business reality. If the Knicks don't extend McBride now, his trade value peaks this season and plummets next summer when he's an expiring contract. Teams won't give up as much for a rental, even a good one. So if Leon Rose believes Deuce is eventually gone, whether because of money or roster redundancy, the smart move is to trade him before the February deadline. Package him with a pick or another young player and go get the third string center they desperately need. Or use him as the salary ballast in a bigger move. That's the logic. But here's the emotional counterargument: this is a championship team. You don't break up championship teams over four million dollar raises. You just don't.
card_lines: Drops next summer as expiring contract
Could fetch rotation C or bigger piece

paragraphs.text: Look at the Knicks' history under Leon Rose. They don't move off key players until contract years. Julius Randle was traded the offseason before he could opt out. Immanuel Quickley was dealt months before restricted free agency. OG Anunoby was allowed to hit free agency because they knew his extension was coming. The pattern is clear: Rose doesn't panic. He waits until the last responsible moment, then acts. That suggests McBride stays through this season unless a can't miss opportunity presents itself. But the lack of extension talks is telling. The Knicks don't have to figure out Deuce's future right now. They have another year on his deal at a rate that makes him almost untouchable from a value standpoint. But if August eleventh comes and goes with no news, the writing is on the wall for next summer.

The wildcard here is what happens if the Knicks think they can get Deuce on a team friendly extension. Something in the fifteen to eighteen million per year range, instead of the full twenty three point seven million annually he could command. That's the dream scenario. Keep the defensive dynamo, maintain financial flexibility, and run it back with the same core. But that requires McBride to take a discount too, after watching Brunson and potentially Towns do the same. At some point, you run out of guys willing to leave money on the table. At some point, the NBPA starts making phone calls. The championship bought the Knicks goodwill. But goodwill has a shelf life in a business where careers end in a torn ACL.

The center position is where the championship tax is already being paid. Mitchell Robinson, the longest tenured Knick before his departure, signed a three year, forty seven point four million dollar deal with the Boston Celtics. The Knicks could have matched that offer in theory, but only by crossing into the second apron that James Dolan has declared radioactive. So Robinson walked. Eight seasons in New York. A second round pick who developed into one of the best rebounders in the league. Gone to a division rival because the owner drew a line in the luxury tax sand. His final act as a Knick was grabbing Josh Hart's missed free throw with twenty six seconds left in Game Five of the Finals, preserving a three point lead. Then he was gone.

The Knicks replaced Robinson with Andre Drummond on a one year, three point nine million dollar deal. Drummond is thirty three years old as of today, actually. Happy birthday, big man. He's the all time leader in career defensive rebounding percentage and total rebounding percentage. Last year he added a real three point shot, hitting thirty five point six percent after a career of being unplayable at the perimeter. He led the playoffs in screen assists per thirty six minutes. On paper, this is a home run value signing. In reality, Drummond is slower than Robinson, a worse rim protector, and shoots forty eight point nine percent from the free throw line for his career. The Athletic's Sam Vecenie said it plainly: Drummond kills the offensive glass and will be valuable in the regular season, but he can't move well enough to be effective in the playoffs.

Think about what that means. The Knicks went from Mitchell Robinson, who was unplayable in some regular season games but critical in the playoffs, to Andre Drummond, who might be the opposite. Drummond started twenty five games for Philly last year when Joel Embiid was hurt. When the Knicks swept the Sixers in the Eastern Conference playoffs, Drummond played a grand total of thirty five minutes across four games. He started Game Two and played only fifteen minutes. That's not a good sign for a player you're counting on as your only backup center. Yes, it's a minimum deal and the Knicks can pivot at the trade deadline. But right now, if Karl-Anthony Towns gets hurt, this team is in trouble.
card_lines: 35 total mins in 2026 vs NYK sweep
Hasn't been playoff rotation C since 2021

paragraphs.text: This is where the McBride trade rumors connect to everything else. If the Knicks move Deuce for a more reliable backup center, someone under contract beyond this season, they solve two problems. They get frontcourt insurance and they avoid paying McBride twenty million per year starting in twenty twenty seven when they're already capped out. But who's available? Moussa Diabate from Charlotte would be perfect, except he's a free agent next summer too. Jalen Smith? Luka Garza? Robert Williams the Third, who's the closest stylistic match to Robinson but has played only eighty five games over three seasons? There's no clean answer. The market is thin, the Knicks are over the first apron, and Dolan won't let them cross the second. They're trying to win a championship with one hand tied behind their back.
card_lines: McBride trade could net better fit

paragraphs.text: The Knicks' second round picks from the twenty twenty six draft are already causing headaches. Jack Kayil, selected thirty ninth overall after New York traded down, is staying in Germany. He signed a five year deal with Alba Berlin, his current team. Kayil is a twenty year old point guard who said he wanted to come to the NBA, but the Knicks' roster crunch left them unable to offer him a standard contract. So he's a draft and stash guy now. Fair enough. The Knicks got him at thirty nine, they have five years of control, and maybe he develops into something overseas. That's fine. The Tyler Nickel situation is messier.
card_lines: Signed 5-year deal to stay in Germany

paragraphs.text: Tyler Nickel, the forty seventh pick from Vanderbilt, is reportedly all in on starting his professional career according to Ian Begley. But there are conflicting reports. James Edwards at The Athletic says Nickel is still considering returning to college for another year after a court ruling granted his class an extra year of eligibility. Here's the problem: Nickel likely needs a standard contract to come to New York, not a two way deal. The Knicks can only afford one more standard contract, and they need that spot for a center. If they give it to Nickel, they can't sign a veteran big. If they don't give it to Nickel, he might go back to school and chase NIL money. The only solution is a trade that opens up space. Which brings us back to Deuce McBride.

The Knicks also lost Jeremy Sochan, the forward they picked up off waivers from San Antonio in February. Sochan signed a one year, non guaranteed deal with the Portland Trail Blazers. He played sixteen regular season games for New York, averaging six point nine minutes and two point eight points. In the playoffs, he saw three point three minutes per game across eight games. He was an emergency depth piece, nothing more. But the fact that the Knicks couldn't even bring back a minimum guy on a non guaranteed deal tells you how tight their books are. They're operating with zero margin for error. Every roster spot is a calculation. Every dollar matters. This is championship team management in the second apron era, and it's ruthless.
card_lines: Knicks too tight to keep minimums

paragraphs.text: Let's zoom out and look at the big picture. The Knicks won the championship. They broke a fifty three year drought. They beat Victor Wembanyama and the Spurs in five games. The city had a parade. This should be the happiest time in franchise history. Instead, the front office is playing financial Tetris just to keep the core together for one more season. James Dolan went on WFAN and said crossing the second apron would be suicidal. That one quote has dictated every decision since. It's why Robinson is gone. It's why Ariel Hukporti signed with Philly. It's why the Knicks are sweating over whether to pay Deuce McBride fifteen million or twenty three million in two years. The new CBA was designed to punish teams like this, and it's working.
card_lines: Lost Robinson, Hukporti to stay under

paragraphs.text: The Knicks are currently about nine million dollars below the second apron. They have fourteen players under contract and need to fill one more standard roster spot, ideally with a center. They've already re-signed Jose Alvarado, Landry Shamet, Mohamed Diawara, and Jordan Clarkson to multiyear deals. Those are good moves. But every one of those contracts eats into the flexibility they need to extend Towns or McBride. Look at the twenty twenty seven to twenty eight cap sheet. The Knicks have nine players under contract and they're already within eight million of the second apron. That's without McBride, without a long term deal for Towns, and without filling out the rest of the roster. The math doesn't work unless somebody takes a massive discount.

Here's the thing that drives me crazy. The Knicks are trying to keep Jalen Brunson, Karl-Anthony Towns, OG Anunoby, Mikal Bridges, and Josh Hart together. That's the core five. That's the group that won the title. But if Towns gets a max extension, even a reduced max, Josh Hart might be the casualty. Hart is under contract through twenty twenty eight on one of the best value deals in the league, but his salary still counts. If the Knicks cross into the second apron, they lose access to the mid level exception, they can't aggregate salaries in trades, and they face harsher penalties for luxury tax payments. So they're stuck. They won the championship by building through trades and smart contracts, and now the same system that rewarded them is threatening to tear it apart.
card_lines: Towns max = Hart could be odd man out

paragraphs.text: This is the new reality of the NBA. You can't keep everyone. You can't just spend your way out of problems. The Thunder couldn't keep everyone and they never even won. The Nuggets are facing the same decisions after their title. The Celtics are navigating it. Every team that builds a winner through trades instead of the draft hits this wall eventually. The Knicks knew this was coming. Leon Rose has been preparing for it since the Brunson extension. But knowing it's coming doesn't make the decisions easier. Tomorrow at midnight, we'll know a little bit more about which direction this is heading. Until then, it's just waiting and hoping that the guys who delivered one championship are willing to sacrifice again to chase another.
card_lines: Thunder, Nuggets, Celtics all facing it

paragraphs.text: Contract extensions and training camp decisions have defined Knicks history, for better and worse. Go back to the summer of nineteen ninety four. The Knicks had just made the Finals, lost to Houston in seven games. Everybody wanted to run it back. Instead, they let Derek Harper walk in free agency, signed over the hill veterans, and the window started closing. Or look at two thousand and eleven. The Knicks traded half the roster for Carmelo Anthony instead of waiting for free agency, gutting their depth and flexibility. Melo got paid, the team never made it past the second round, and the franchise wandered in the wilderness for a decade. These extension decisions echo through time. Get them right, you stay competitive. Get them wrong, you waste a championship core.

The flip side is the nineteen seventy three championship team. That squad was built on smart, team friendly deals and guys who prioritized winning. Walt Frazier, Willis Reed, Earl Monroe, Dave DeBusschere, Bill Bradley. None of them were the highest paid at their position. They played together because they wanted to win, and because Red Holzman and the front office kept the band together through intelligent roster management. That's the model the current Knicks are chasing. That's why they're asking Towns and McBride to take less. But the salary cap didn't exist in nineteen seventy three. The second apron wasn't a thing. The comparison only goes so far when the league itself has changed the rules to prevent dynasty building.
card_lines: No salary cap or apron then

paragraphs.text: Training camps are about to start in less than two months. Preseason games begin shortly after. The Knicks will face the Raptors twice in exhibition play, with a possible matchup against LeBron James and the Sixers still on the table. Media day is expected in late September. By then, we'll know whether Deuce McBride got extended or is playing on an expiring contract. We'll know whether Towns took a discount or is betting on himself for one more year. We'll know if the Knicks added another center or if they're rolling with Drummond as the only backup. All of these decisions will be made in the next few weeks, with tomorrow's deadline kicking off the final chapter of the offseason. The championship hangover is officially over. Business is back.

At the end of the day, this all comes back to one question: how badly does everyone want to stay together? The Knicks clearly want to keep the core intact. Leon Rose has said it. The players have said it. The moves they've made, from extending Brunson early to bringing back Alvarado and Shamet, all point toward continuity. But wanting it and affording it are two different things. The second apron isn't a suggestion. It's a hard cap with real penalties. If the Knicks cross it, they lose roster building tools for years. If they stay under it, they lose players. There's no perfect answer. There's only choosing which pain you can live with.
card_lines: How badly does everyone want to stay?

paragraphs.text: Deuce McBride and Karl-Anthony Towns are going to get paid. The only question is whether they get paid by the Knicks, and how much they're willing to sacrifice to make it happen. Tomorrow we'll have more clarity. Not answers, necessarily. But clarity. If both guys let the deadline pass without extensions, we'll know they're prioritizing security over team flexibility. And honestly, who could blame them? This is a business. Careers are short. Injuries are random. You take care of yourself first, because the team will move on the second it's convenient. We've seen it a thousand times. The Knicks just let Mitchell Robinson walk after eight years and a championship. They'll do it again if the numbers don't work. That's not cruelty. That's professional sports.

So here we are. August tenth, twenty twenty six. The Knicks are defending champions, trying to navigate the most punishing collective bargaining agreement in NBA history. They're asking their stars to take less. They're letting beloved players walk. They're sweating over whether to give their backup point guard fifteen million or twenty million in two years. This is the cost of winning. This is what happens when you build a champion through trades and shrewd signings instead of tanking for draft picks. The pressure is immense. The margin for error is zero. And tomorrow, at midnight, the first domino falls. Buckle up, Knicks fans. The offseason just got very, very real. We'll be watching every move, every report, every hint of which direction this front office is leaning. Because the next twenty four hours might determine whether this championship was the beginning of a dynasty, or the peak of a short, brilliant window.
card_lines: Most punishing CBA in NBA history
